title: Negative information questions with singular action verbs
summary: Use the question word, the appropriate negative verb and the main verb's negative form: Miksi sinä et tule? Miksi sinä et tule? — Koska olen sairas.
targetSkills: Negative information questions with singular action verbs
prerequisiteSkills: Negative information questions with plural olla forms
objectives: Build a singular negative action question without an extra question suffix.
Use the unchanged negative main-verb form and give an appropriate information reply.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
A stem is the part of a word to which an ending is attached.
The partitive is a word form used here for an amount, an action's object, or a substance or group description.
The illative is an into/to form; mihin aikaan uses that form in a time expression.
An adjective is a word that describes a quality.
A pronoun stands in place of a name or noun.
A weak stem uses the changed consonants shown in the construction steps; the strong stem keeps the corresponding strong consonants.

Use the question word, the appropriate negative verb and the main verb's negative form: Miksi sinä et tule? (“Why aren't you coming?”). Form these negative main-verb forms by removing -n from the supplied I-form: tulen → tule, juon → juo, luen → lue. The negative form keeps the stem changes already present in the I-form.
keyPoints: After the question word use et or ei, not etkö/eikö and not an affirmative verb.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: For a negative reply, change the addressed person's et into your en and keep the main verb's negative form: En juo kahvia (“I do not drink coffee”). Negative action objects use the partitive in these examples. The complete noun forms are supplied because object formation is not this lesson's target.
A natural short reply to “Miksi sinä et tule?” is “Koska olen sairas.” (“Because I am ill.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: Do not add a personal ending to the main verb after en or ei.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: olen means I am here. Olla has the I-form olen: ole- + -n. The ending identifies the speaker.
on means is here. Olla has the irregular singular third-person form on.
en means I do not here. En is the first-person singular negative verb. The main verb takes its negative form.

juo means drink here. Juoda removes -da to form juo. This is the singular third-person affirmative form and, after a negative verb, the negative main-verb form; the long vowel does not lengthen further.
syö means eat here. Syödä removes -dä to form syö, used as the singular third-person affirmative form or as the main verb after a negative verb.
tule means come here. Remove -n from tulen to obtain the negative main-verb form tule; the negative verb carries the person.
mene means go here. Remove -n from menen to obtain negative mene, unchanged after every present negative verb.
lue means read here. Remove -n from luen to obtain negative lue. Keep the weak stem with k absent.
keyPoints: Do not add a personal ending to the main verb after en or ei.

steps: Miksi: why; question asking for a reason. Miksi asks for a reason.

olen: I am; verb (the action or state). Olla has the I-form olen: ole- + -n. The ending identifies the speaker.

Minä: I; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Minä is the singular first-person subject pronoun, used by a speaker about themself.

kirjastoon: to the library; destination. Repeat the final o and add n: kirjasto + o + n gives kirjastoon.
